title: Work Techniques · L1 Medical vocabulary and word formation

questions.stem: According to the lecture, medical vocabulary:
options: Is made of arbitrary lexical forms
Is a rule-governed morphological system based on Greek and Latin
Should be learned by analytical decoding rather than rote memorization
questions.explanation: Meaning is systematically encoded through standardized word parts, not arbitrary forms.

questions.stem: Match the component to its role:
options: Root — semantic core of the term
Combining vowel — carries the main meaning
questions.explanation: The combining vowel has no meaning of its own; it is a morphophonemic connector.

options: It changes the meaning of the root
It has no semantic meaning of its own
questions.explanation: In cardi/o/logy or gastr/o/enter/o/logy, "o" is purely a linking element.

questions.stem: Which root–meaning pairs are given in the lecture?

questions.explanation: dys- = abnormal or impaired; hyper- = excessive.

questions.stem: Hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia, or tachycardia and bradycardia, show that:
options: The suffix always decides the meaning alone
Opposite conditions can be distinguished only by the prefix
Prefixes can be core diagnostic indicators
questions.explanation: The lecture concludes that prefixes are not auxiliary elements but core diagnostic indicators.

questions.stem: According to the lecture, which component is often the most diagnostically significant?
questions.explanation: Suffixes define the grammatical and clinical category (inflammation, procedure, condition, field) and are often the most diagnostically significant component.

questions.stem: About Greek and Latin in medical English:
options: Latin is more common for anatomical structures and descriptive terms
The dual system produces parallel forms for related concepts
Greek is mainly associated with diagnostic, pathological and functional terms
Greek is mainly used for anatomy
questions.explanation: e.g. cardiac (Latin-based descriptive adjective) vs cardiology (Greek-based discipline).

questions.stem: Match the word to the formation process given in the lecture:
questions.explanation: cardiology → cardiologist → cardiac → cardiopathy illustrates derivational morphology (a lexical family from one root).

questions.stem: In the lexical family cardiology → cardiologist → cardiac → cardiopathy:
options: cardiology is the field of study

questions.stem: What is the order of the lecture's decoding model?
questions.explanation: The suffix comes first because it is the most stable marker and narrows the interpretive domain.

questions.stem: In step 2 of the decoding model, prefixes may indicate:
options: The diagnostic frame of the term (disease, procedure)
questions.explanation: The diagnostic frame is given by the suffix (step 1). Prefixes also mark time/function (pre-, post-).

options: Abnormally high concentration of glucose in the blood

questions.stem: Which are examples of irregularities in medical terminology given in the lecture?
questions.explanation: Irregularities come from historical borrowing, clinical conventions, international variation and abbreviation systems.

questions.stem: Which study strategies does the lecture recommend for learning medical vocabulary?
options: Contextual exposure through authentic clinical texts
Rote memorization of isolated word lists
questions.explanation: The lecture calls for a shift from rote memorization toward analysis, plus morphological mapping and active retrieval.
